title: V.I.B.E.
content:
Elena Zaghis is a writer based in the Netherlands:

Founded in 2021, Do Not Research is a reader-supported publication. Each week, we highlight the work of an artist or writer:

team: August Kasa Sundgaard au.dust, Giulia Timis ju_mping, Caitlin Van Bommel casitlin, Elena Zaghis 666ultracorpo999 — collaborators: Shao-Chun Hsu hsuuusc [fabrication], Claudio Castro Chaponan [coding]

Vibe Politics

Contemporary political influence announces itself as spiritual warfare wrapped in kawaii aesthetics.

/\___ /\
꒰ ˶• ༝ - ˶꒱
./づᡕᠵ᠊$◌࡚ࠢ࠘ ⸝!!᠊◌࠘߯ ᠆࠘ࠣᡁࠣ ᠊᠊°. ——————~ ✶

The manifestos read like fan fictions—all live-laugh-lovers practicing what they call “network spirituality,” the futurist embrace of experiential hyperreality found in the web’s accelerated matrix. Playful language camouflages nine-figure political machines. Behind the cuteness: lobbying, coalition-building, systematic influence campaigns cloaked in mystical language and “post-authorship” to evade accountability.

What we’re witnessing goes beyond the aestheticization of politics that Walter Benjamin warned about. Digital platforms don’t just distribute propaganda at scale; they restructure the conditions under which anything counts as persuasive. The logic of print culture—linear argument, detached reason, verifiable facts—has given way to something closer to oral culture’s immediacy, performance, and emotional resonance. Except now it operates at algorithmic speed, through screens instead of village squares. An epistemic mutation is underway—a shift in how political truth gets made and circulated.

Today’s political movements win not through substantive debate but through constructed vibes. They exploit the gap between how politics appear (kawaii UwU online angels, friendly chakra viruses) and how they function (investment funds, lobbying, algorithmic warfare). While self-described net warriors position themselves as artsy schizo-posters, we still lack tools to analyze how ambient propaganda actually operates—not as discrete messages to be fact-checked, but as atmospheric conditions that shape what feels true before anyone starts thinking.

V.I.B.E. (VIRAL IDEOLOGY BROADCAST EXPERIMENT) is a speculative electoral campaign rendered as an interactive installation, featuring physical voting booths, screens and election-related materials. It presents an overwhelming audiovisual environment using fragmented, repetitive video clips that mix social media imagery, anime characters, angels, cute pastels, with disturbingly fascist affirmations. This deliberate overload of conflicting elements bombards the viewer, mirroring political strategies that bypass rational argument in favor of affective influence. The installation doesn’t just represent how modern politics work—it simulates the mechanism itself, building moods and feelings instead of relying on factual arguments. Over the past year, it has been shown at Ars Electronica in Linz, Mozilla Festival in Barcelona, Dutch Design Week in Eindhoven, and the Institute of Network Cultures in Amsterdam.

This is vibe culture as epistemology: a wholesale replacement of how political knowledge gets produced and legitimated. In a media landscape dominated by algorithmic feeds and short-form video, rational discourse doesn’t just get outcompeted—it becomes structurally illegible. Platforms don’t have opinions about truth; they have architectures that determine what spreads. And what spreads is what resonates, not what withstands scrutiny.

The far-right has weaponized this shift most effectively: blending cuteness with violence, aesthetics with ideology, exploiting platform architectures that reward emotional resonance over logical coherence. Chibi girls and e-angels hint at something sinister beneath the surface, but the surface is the message. Through memetic saturation, tech-obsessed Landian politics advances not through persuasion but through atmospheric takeover.

You can’t fact-check a vibe. You can’t debate a feeling. The affective registers these movements operate through—the cute, the edgy, the mystical, the accelerationist—function as ideological delivery systems that smuggle far-right politics past the defenses of critical thinking. The transformation runs deeper than straight forward manipulation: it reshapes what counts as convincing in the first place.

The Dynasty Mindset

Within hyperonline far-right movements—those blending kawaii aesthetics with authoritarian politics—one aesthetic strategy recurs with particular intensity: the obsession with China as what one manifesto describes as the fulcrum of “mutually assured technological acceleration.” This manifests visually through ideograms and imperial Chinese iconography—what gets called the “Dynasty Mindset”—deployed to construct a sense of ideological power and historical inevitability.

This appropriation of Chinese imperial symbols extends beyond to encompass Japanese anime aesthetics, Christian mystical imagery, and Silicon Valley tech-bro iconography, creating a syncretic visual language that appears culturally inclusive while serving exclusionary political ends. It’s cosmopolitan aesthetics in service of nationalist politics, it’s multicultural imagery weaponized for monoculture. The Dynasty Mindset performs global fluency while actually operating as ideological consolidation—emperors and acceleration, tradition and tech, all compressed into memetic shorthand.

What makes this strategy effective is precisely its incoherence. The symbols don’t need to mean anything consistent—they just need to resonate. Imperial China signifies strength, discipline, hierarchy. Anime signals ironic distance and subcultural fluency. Christian mysticism adds transcendent legitimacy. Silicon Valley tech-worship promises inevitable futures. Together, they create an affective collage that feels powerful without requiring logical integration. This is vibe politics in its purest form: meaning as mood, ideology as aesthetic accumulation.

Benjamin warned that “all efforts to render politics aesthetic culminate in one thing: war.” But in the platform age, that warning needs updating. When politics becomes primarily aesthetic, war doesn’t arrive as a climax—it becomes ambient, continuous, atmospheric. Cute angels and imperial aesthetics are the weapons. Your capacity to distinguish between feeling something and knowing it is the casualty.

Politicians succeed not by persuading across lines of difference but by performing loyalty to a tribe. Rational debate gives way to memetic warfare. Argument becomes vibe.

Ambient Propaganda Infrastructure

In the platform age—characterized by algorithmic curation, endless scroll, and the collapse of shared epistemic ground. Algorithmic feeds reward emotional resonance over logical coherence. Short-form video privileges affect over-argument. The timeline itself becomes an ambient propaganda machine, training users to process politics as vibes rather than positions.

The epistemic architecture matters more than content moderation or misinformation takedowns. Platforms optimize for engagement, which means they optimize for emotional intensity. Outrage travels faster than nuance. Tribal signaling outcompetes cross-partisan dialogue. The cute-violent aesthetic cocktail that characterizes contemporary far-right movements isn’t just effective despite platform logic—it’s effective because of it.

The schizo-poster aesthetic—mixing sincere devotion with ironic distance, high theory with low memes—creates plausible deniability while maintaining ideological coherence. You can always claim it’s just a joke, just aesthetics, just vibes. But the cumulative effect is atmospheric saturation. Politics becomes something you feel in the scroll, not something you deliberate about. Network spirituality, post-authorship, mutually assured technological acceleration: these function as strategic frameworks for evading accountability while building influence.

When everything is vibes and nothing is attributable, how do you organize resistance? When politics operates primarily through ambient saturation rather than explicit argument, what does critical analysis even look like?

Critical Adjacency

Traditional critical tools—demystification, ideology critique, revealing the hidden mechanisms—struggle against this mode of politics. The mechanisms aren’t hidden—they’re already aestheticized, already incorporated into the vibe. Exposing that the cute angels are a fascist psyop doesn’t neutralize them. In some contexts, it might even enhance their edgy appeal, confirming their transgressive credentials.

What V.I.B.E. attempts instead is critical adjacency: reproducing the aesthetic environment so faithfully that viewers experience its operation firsthand. The installation makes you feel how vibe politics works rather than explaining it. It constructs what it critiques, occupying the same registers of mystification while making that mystification legible through saturation and overload.

Methodologically, this is a risky territory. Reproduce the aesthetic too faithfully and you become indistinguishable from what you’re analyzing—potentially amplifying rather than questioning. Aestheticize the critique itself and you might replicate the problem at a meta level. But the alternative—maintaining critical distance, refusing aesthetic engagement, treating politics as if they still operate through rational argument—means ceding the entire territory of affect to whoever’s weaponizing them.

V.I.B.E.’s answer is architectural: create an environment where the mechanisms of vibe politics become perceptible through excess. When the angels, and pastels, and imperial aesthetics are layered too thickly, when the voting booths sit too close to the fascist symbolism, when the cute violence accumulates past the point of comfortable irony—that’s when the infrastructure becomes visible as ambient condition to be inhabited and recognized, rather than hidden machinery requiring revelation.

We need methods for analyzing ambient propaganda that don’t force us to pretend we’re somehow outside its reach. The post-truth era proliferates incompatible reality tunnels, each with its own internal coherence, each optimized for different affective responses. Vibe culture wins not by being more true but by being more compelling, more shareable, more memetically fit.

The infrastructure that enables it—the platforms that reward engagement over accuracy, the algorithmic feeds that prioritize emotion over evidence, the attention economy that treats politics as content—affects everyone. We’re all swimming in ambient propaganda. The question is whether we can develop analytical literacies adequate to this environment, or whether we’ll keep mistaking vibes for arguments, feelings for facts, aesthetic power for actual power.

Fact-checking and media literacy campaigns can’t reverse the epistemic shift. Those tools assume a shared commitment to verification that no longer exists as common ground.

When different publics don’t just disagree but operate with fundamentally incompatible understandings of what counts as evidence, you can’t debate your way back to consensus. The transformation is deeper: a mutation in how political truth gets made, circulated, and felt.

What does it feel like to be targeted by vibe politics? And once you recognize that feeling—the way affect bypasses cognition, the way spectacle displaces substance while maintaining democratic aesthetics—can you still pretend it’s just content, just vibes, just aesthetics?

Welcome to the affective battlefield. Your timeline has already picked sides. The question now is whether critical analysis can catch up to the infrastructure, or whether we’ll keep treating vibe politics as a distortion of democracy rather than its mutation into something we don’t yet have language for.
